1:
Gill sets the scene: the promise of God fulfilled, the land for the most part subdued, the war at an end, and the nine tribes and a half settled in quiet possession of their lots — whereupon Joshua sends for the men who had taken their portion beyond Jordan at their own request and crossed over armed to help their brethren. Henry sees a prudent general disbanding an army that never designed to make war its trade, sending the men home to beat their swords into ploughshares. Calvin presses the awkward question the discharge raises: how can Joshua reckon their service done while the enemy still holds part of the land, the sole possession of which ought to have been the war's proper end? His answer puts the fault elsewhere. Had Israel seconded God's agency instead of drawing back when he stretched out his hand, the remainder would have been finished with no danger and little trouble; and since from their own sloth they refused what God was ready to bestow, the agreement by which the two tribes and a half had bound themselves ceased to bind.

How long they had served, and whether they saw their homes in the interval, is disputed. Henry cites the best chronologers for six or seven years, and thinks it probable that when the rest of the army retired into winter quarters some at least stepped over Jordan — it was not far — to visit their families and look to their affairs, sending others in their room, the quota of forty thousand being always ready at its posts. Clarke puts the war at seven years and draws the opposite inference: though only the river lay between the camp and their inheritance, fordable at every season but harvest, it does not appear that they ever once revisited home. Gill reports the Jewish reckoning of fourteen years, seven in subduing the land and seven in dividing it; Calvin, who gives the same figure, praises them for waiting quietly to be sent for.

Henry ranks the commendation under three heads: readiness of obedience, which he calls the soldier's praise above all; constancy of adherence, since they had not left their brethren all those days; and faithfulness to the divine law — you have kept the keeping — by which he understands that they had kept up religion in their part of the camp, a rare and excellent thing among soldiers. Keil and Delitzsch read the clause more narrowly, as observing what had to be observed with respect to the commandment, and set the repetition about Manasseh's two halves down to the copious breadth of early Hebrew historical style. The counsel Joshua then gives is not political but pious, Henry observes: nothing of fortifying cities or enlarging territory, only diligent heed to do the commandment. Calvin finds its force in its permanence: Joshua releases them from temporary service in order to bind them for ever to the one true God, so that wherever they are they remain his soldiers. Clarke takes the clauses one by one, cleaving as a union never to be dissolved, and holds that without an affectionate filial attachment to the Maker duty would be irksome and impossible; Wesley reduces commandment and law to two words for one thing.

Whether the tribes who stayed behind had any claim on the plunder divides the rest. Calvin holds they could not honestly have demanded it, having borne none of the toil or danger; Joshua does not insist on the legal view but exhorts liberality, asking not an equal partition but enough to remove all cause of envy. Clarke thinks the share plainly due, since without the men who defended the families and tilled the ground the others could not have safely left home at all. Wesley agrees, but denies the portions were equal, contrasting the later case in which the danger had been equal too.
10:
Gill reads the Geliloth of the border as the meanders and turnings of the river near Jericho. Henry knows the opinion that the altar stood on the Canaan side in Benjamin's lot, so that the builders might see the figure of the altar at Shiloh across the water when they could not conveniently go to it, but thinks it likelier they built on their own side — what had they to do to build on another man's land without his consent? — and adds that there would have been no ground of suspicion at all had they not built it among themselves. Wesley repeats the argument almost word for word, and Clarke insists the west bank can never be meant, being neither their territory nor of any use to their own people for worship. Ellicott also prefers the east, finding in the description a reminder of the very thing the altar was to enforce, that both borders of Jordan belong to the promised land, though he notes a proposed site twenty miles north of Jericho on the western bank. Keil and Delitzsch reconcile the two descriptions by taking Canaan in a restricted sense that stops at the Jordan valley.

Ellicott insists the text means the altar — a copy of the one altar given to Israel for sacrifice, set up as a likeness on the east so that the tribes there might appeal to it as proof that they too were the people of Jehovah. Henry allows the motive entirely, the care of the separated tribes to keep their hold of Canaan's religion and a bridge to keep up their fellowship in the things of God, but faults the discretion: having made a thing with an appearance of evil, they should have consulted the oracle, or at least told their brethren beforehand, giving the explanation to prevent the jealousy rather than to remove it. Calvin presses the same charge harder. Nothing was farther from their intention than to innovate, yet they sinned not lightly in attempting a novelty without any regard to the high priest, and in a form very liable to be misconstrued; from which he takes the apostle's rule that one must attend not only to what is lawful but to what is expedient.

Calvin then defends the vehemence of the other side. It should not seem excessive to take up arms against their own blood over a pile of stones, since they judged truly that a second place of sacrifice would profane the worship and open a door to superstition. Yet he grants the zeal was not free from turbulent impetuosity, since they made ready for war before inquiring. Henry calls the suspicion excusable, the thing looking ill at first sight, and the prudence no less commendable, God having commanded them in such a case to inquire and make search, lest they wrong their brethren under pretence of righting their religion.

The charge itself is high, and Henry says plainly that it is well they were not able to make it good. Gill observes that Peor was a single act whereas an altar is built for continuance; Wesley grants that God had pardoned the national punishment while the blot and the corrupt leaven remained; Keil and Delitzsch answer that the plague had in fact avenged that guilt, so Phinehas cannot have meant it was unpunished. Both Henry and Clarke dwell on the offer that closes the speech, that rather than let their brethren feel the want of an altar the western tribes would straiten themselves and give up part of their own allotted land — the spirit, Henry says, of Israelites indeed. Ellicott finds in the whole scene the strongest proof of the narrative's antiquity, since no writer of Jeremiah's day, when altars to Baal were as many as the streets, could have conceived a single rival altar to Jehovah as cause for war.
21:
Clarke thinks the manner of the answer as creditable as its matter: conscious of their own innocence, the accused let Phinehas finish a discourse composed of little else than accusations, and he wishes some public assemblies of his own day that lay claim to the highest refinement would take the lesson. Henry finds the reply fair and ingenuous. They do not retort the charge, nor upbraid their brethren with the injustice of their threatenings, nor demur to their jurisdiction and bid them mind their own business, but give a soft answer that turns away wrath. Calvin makes the same restraint a rule: when a thing rightly done is falsely blamed by those who do not understand it, it may be enough to refute the censure only so far as clears ourselves.

The state of the case, Calvin says, turns on a definition, and the builders begin by putting the wickedness they were suspected of as far from them as an oath can. Keil and Delitzsch set out the three names heaped together — the strong one, the Supreme Being to be feared, and the truly existing covenant God — and note that the invocation is strengthened further by repeating all three. Clarke calls the words exceedingly emphatic and hardly translatable, coming nearest in Luther's rendering, and holds that nothing but the utmost consciousness of integrity could have induced men to add, save us not this day. Gill takes the repetition for steadiness of faith and vehement affection for the truth; Wesley for zeal, and finds in that last clause a sudden apostrophe to God such as vehement speech runs into. Calvin adds that strictly one cannot set God above other gods, there being no others to compare him with, and that the phrase is framed to the common sense of ordinary men.

Their reason was fear for their posterity. Henry describes the thought as arising on the journey home — not before, or they would have told Joshua — and finds in the text a word signifying great perplexity of mind: distance and the river would keep their children from the yearly feasts, so that they would be reckoned inconsiderable members of the church and by degrees rejected as none at all. Your children, in their pride, will monopolize the privileges of the altar, and ours, perhaps not careful enough to keep hold of them, will cease from fearing the Lord. Henry's rule follows, that the form and profession of godliness may be kept without the life and power, but the life and power will not long be kept without the form — you take away grace if you take away the means of grace. Wesley repeats it. Gill goes behind the fear to the premise it rested on: Jordan was indeed the eastern border of Canaan strictly so called, but the land beyond it was no less promised to Abraham, the Amorites driven out of it having been Canaanites too.

On what the altar actually was the rest converge. Ellicott insists on the pattern or copy of the altar of Jehovah, proving the eastern tribes' equal right to approach him; Clarke says it served no religious purpose but testified that they were one people under one constitution. Calvin meets the objection that the law forbids such erections by observing that only images meant to represent God are condemned, a heap of stones raised as a trophy or memorial being nowhere prohibited — otherwise Joshua and many holy judges after him would have defiled themselves. Ellicott traces the taunt the builders feared through Ephraim's abuse of the Gileadites to Jeroboam's calves, and then turns it on his own day: there are altars still that occasion dispute, and it would tend greatly to peace if we could be assured that, like this one, they are not for sacrifice but for a witness.
30:
Henry credits the outcome to a disposition to peace on both sides matching the zeal for God on both sides, since quarrels about religion, for want of wisdom and love, often prove the fiercest and the hardest to make up. He notes three things the ambassadors did not do: they did not question the sincerity of the protestation, charity believing and hoping the best; they did not upbraid the builders with the rashness that had cost an embassy, a little want of consideration being excusable in men who plainly mean honestly; and they did not go fishing for evidence to make good a charge merely because they had once made it. Calvin draws the same lesson as a warning against obstinacy. Many men, once offended, cannot be appeased by any defence and will find something to carp at rather than seem to yield to reason, whereas these were ready instantly to take an equitable view of a matter they had not understood.

Phinehas reads the innocence as a token of the divine presence. Keil and Delitzsch give his sense plainly: because you have not been unfaithful, we know Jehovah is among us, and you have preserved Israel from his judgments. Clarke reports the Targum's paraphrase, in which the majesty of the Lord dwells among them and the trespass would have been against the Word of the Lord, and finds a promise in the conclusion as well, that a God present as the sole object of worship will abide as protector and portion. Wesley makes the deliverance a matter of prevention, since he that prevents an approaching mischief delivers a man as truly as he that removes it after it has fallen. Ellicott adds that the best token of the divine presence among men is the divine likeness in men. Calvin turns the sentence into a doctrine: we never revolt unless God has first abandoned us, and we persevere only so far as he sustains us by his hand.

The altar was left standing. Henry observes that Joshua and the princes did not order it demolished, though there was as much reason to fear it might in time occasion idolatry as to hope it would prevent it — the strong bearing the infirmities of the weak — and that the one precaution taken was to record the explanation in a name. Gill supposes the word inscribed or engraved upon it. Clarke notes that the name is absent from the common Hebrew editions and supplied in italics by the translators, though it is found in several manuscripts and in the Syriac and Arabic, and must be allowed necessary to complete the sense. Keil and Delitzsch treat the clause as at once a name and its own explanation. Wesley and Ellicott alike make the confession universal: Jehovah is God, of all the twelve tribes alike.

Clarke closes with an excursus on the schism the whole chapter turned upon. The word should be well understood: it means a rent in the doctrine and practice of the apostles among those once united in it, so that departure from merely human institutions is no schism at all, the Word of God being the sufficient rule and one party's forms as good as another's. Dissent that makes no rent in the essentials he refuses to call by the name. What he condemns is separation to set up one non-essential form in the place of another, since both sides must then magnify the difference beyond all reason, tithing mint and cummin while the weightier matters go neglected. If Christians cannot think alike on all points, he says, they can agree to disagree; and he denies that this breeds indifference, since in the essentials we should ever be zealously affected.
